title: Recent strengthening of eastern Pacific ENSO in the last millennium paleorecord.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded all 15 data files (600 KB total) from the NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information paleoclimatology archive, study 43983 (dataset DOI 10.25921/c99k-mk95), and parsed every one. Each is a tab-separated text file with exactly three numeric columns: Calendar_year (year CE), Sr/Ca (strontium-to-calcium ratio, millimole per mole) and d18O (oxygen-isotope ratio, per mil). Counted 7,308 data rows in total and the year range of each core; confirmed by text search that no sea-surface-temperature or El Nino index column appears in any file. Also confirmed the Zenodo hit returned for this DOI ('el-nino-amplification-utac', GenesisAeon) is unrelated third-party software, not the authors' data.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The Science article itself is paywalled with no PubMed Central copy (Europe PMC: isOpenAccess=N, inEPMC=N), and science.org returned HTTP 403, so the methods, supplementary materials and any stated record counts were never read. Everything about how the chronologies were built, how Sr/Ca was converted to temperature, and which comparison paleorecords and climate-model runs were used comes only from the abstract reproduced in the NOAA file headers.

a1_downloadable.note: All 15 files downloaded with no login from the NOAA archive; 600 KB total, public domain US government data.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAIL. The files contain only year, Sr/Ca and d18O. The thing anyone would predict here - sea surface temperature, or an El Nino/Southern Oscillation index - is in no column. It must be constructed by joining each coral's depth-derived calendar date to an external gridded sea-surface-temperature product (for example ERSSTv5 or HadISST) at the island's coordinates, which is a spatial-temporal interpolation, not a key join, and only exists after about 1870.

a3_inputs_present.note: Inputs are the measured numbers themselves, present in every row; no identifier lookup needed. Verified in the files.

a4_units_stated.note: Units and analytical precision are declared in each header: Sr/Ca in millimole per mole (precision +/-0.02, inductively-coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy), d18O in per mil (precision +/-0.08, isotope ratio mass spectrometry). Verified in the files.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAIL in disguise, the same way the scCT-DB candidate failed. 7,308 monthly rows look ample, but the independent unit is the coral core, and there are 15 of them from 5 Galapagos islands, falling in roughly 10 non-overlapping time windows (1129-1167, 1335-1358, 1420-1447, 1570-1615, 1681-1717, 1757-1780, 1783-1835, 1863-1983, 1941-1983, 1985-2015). Monthly values within one core are strongly autocorrelated, and only ~3,300 rows sit in the instrumental era where any temperature label could exist at all. Counted in the files.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: 0.6 MB of coral data; about 1 GB more if a gridded sea-surface-temperature product were added
a6_fits_laptop.note: Trivially laptop-sized; measured the downloaded files.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: No disagreement found, but only weakly checked: the archive lists 15 files and 15 downloaded and parsed. The paper's own record count could not be compared because the full text is paywalled.

a8_label_provenance.note: FAIL for the natural label. Any temperature target would come from a gridded sea-surface-temperature analysis, and over the Galapagos before the 1980s satellite era those grids are statistically infilled reconstructions, not direct measurements - so the label is partly another model's output. The alternative, deriving temperature from Sr/Ca with a published calibration equation, computes the label from the feature, which is leakage by construction.

existing_models.name: Grouped machine-learning reconstruction of seawater d18O from paired coral Sr/Ca and d18O (reproducible workflow, Zenodo record 22027756, published 2026-08-20, CC-BY-4.0)
existing_models.score_and_split: Skill numbers not verified - I retrieved only the Zenodo record metadata, not the manuscript. The record describes grouped machine learning with explicit site-group assignments and pseudoproxy experiments over 53 paired CoralHydro2k records, i.e. a held-out-site split rather than a random one.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: The title states the finding: the choice of calibration target itself limits how well machine learning can reconstruct from paired coral Sr/Ca and d18O.

existing_models.name: Deep-learning tropical Pacific data assimilation of coral proxies (Meng et al., Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems 2024; arXiv 2406.07063)
existing_models.score_and_split: Not verified - seen only as a search listing with the claim that assimilating with the deep-learning model beats a Linear Inverse Model for averaging times of 1 month to 1 year. I did not retrieve the paper.

existing_models.name: A Comprehensive Evaluation of Machine Learning on Coral Trace Element Paleothermometers for Sea Surface Temperature Reconstruction
existing_models.score_and_split: Not verified - title and venue appeared in a search listing only; the paper was not retrieved, so no number is claimed.

backbone.name: None
backbone.hardware: CPU only, but irrelevant - no pretrained backbone exists for two-channel coral geochemical time series, and none of the approved biology backbones (ESM-2, ChemBERTa, AlphaGenome, Nucleotide Transformer, scGPT, RNA-FM) takes this input type.

integration.partner_dataset: CoralHydro2k (the PAGES compilation of paired coral Sr/Ca and d18O records for the last 2,000 years) and a gridded sea-surface-temperature product such as ERSSTv5
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does a temperature calibration fitted on modern corals still hold for fossil corals grown centuries earlier - the question is real, but the Zenodo workflow above already attacks it with 53 paired CoralHydro2k records, more than three times this paper's 15 cores.

controls.positive_control: Available in principle: the 1982-83 and 1997-98 El Nino events are textbook features that any working pipeline must recover as warm anomalies in the modern cores (dar1532top, wlf1003top, wlf1010).
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling is runnable, but on 15 autocorrelated series it would mostly test the block structure of the shuffle rather than the model.
controls.external_validation: CoralHydro2k and the companion Tripp et al. 2026 Geophysical Research Letters mid-Holocene records would serve, and both are independent of this archive.

honest_claim_h3: A model trained on these files could at best claim: given monthly strontium-to-calcium and oxygen-isotope values from a Porites lobata colony at one of five Galapagos islands, it reproduces the sea-surface temperature that a gridded reconstruction assigns to that island in that month - a claim about agreement with another reconstruction over about 10 disjoint time windows and 15 coral colonies, not about temperature itself.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use coral skeleton chemistry to predict the ocean temperature the coral grew in, back through the last millennium.
plain_idea.train_on: Monthly strontium-to-calcium ratios and oxygen-isotope ratios measured along 15 Galapagos coral cores; 7,308 rows verified in the files, of which about 3,300 fall in the era when instrumental temperatures exist.
plain_idea.predict: Sea surface temperature, or whether a given year was an El Nino year. The true answer is not in these files - it would have to come from a gridded temperature product such as ERSSTv5, which over the Galapagos before the satellite era is itself an infilled statistical reconstruction rather than a measurement.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Paleoclimatologists want to know whether the chemistry-to-temperature calibration fitted on living corals is valid for fossil corals grown centuries earlier, because every statement about past El Nino strength rests on that assumption. Even a failure would quantify how far the calibration can be pushed.

more_or_better_data.why: This archive holds 15 coral cores; the open Zenodo workflow from August 2026 already uses 53 paired Sr/Ca-d18O records from CoralHydro2k, and these Galapagos cores will themselves be folded into that compilation.

confidence_score.why: The headers state analytical precision (+/-0.02 millimole per mole for Sr/Ca, +/-0.08 per mil for d18O), which bounds measurement noise, but there are no replicate cores covering the same years for most windows, so calibration uncertainty across colonies cannot be estimated from these files alone.

models_beatable.why: The directly comparable work is from 2026, uses grouped site-level splits and pseudoproxy experiments, and ships a CC-BY reproducible Python workflow - open code plus an honest split is exactly the combination the checklist calls fatal.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Multiple conditions fail: our model would not see everything theirs sees, the temperature target is not measured the same way across the instrumental and pre-instrumental periods, and no shared evaluation split exists.

ml_idea: The considered project was: predict monthly sea surface temperature (or El Nino event occurrence) from paired coral strontium-to-calcium and oxygen-isotope values, train on the modern Galapagos cores that overlap the instrumental record, and test how far that calibration transfers to the fossil cores from earlier centuries. Rejected: the target is in no column and must be built from an external gridded temperature product that is itself partly a reconstruction, the independent unit is 15 coral cores rather than 7,308 monthly rows, no pretrained backbone fits this data type, and an open reproducible machine-learning workflow on 53 paired coral records already exists.

effort.compute_note: Measured: the 15 files total 600 KB and parsed in under a second with the standard library. The 6 hours is an estimate dominated by aligning coral calendar dates to a gridded sea-surface-temperature product, not by concatenating the files, which takes minutes.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Open any one file and list its columns - there are three (Calendar_year, Sr/Ca, d18O) and none of them is temperature. That one command, which took under a minute, kills the project.

verdict_reason: Part A fails three ways. A2: the prediction target (sea surface temperature or an El Nino index) is in no column of any of the 15 files I downloaded and parsed - it would have to be constructed by joining coral dates to an external gridded temperature product. A8: that product is itself an infilled statistical reconstruction over the Galapagos before the satellite era, so the label is partly another model's output, while the alternative (applying a published Sr/Ca-to-temperature equation) computes the label from the feature. A5: 7,308 monthly rows reduce to 15 autocorrelated coral cores in about 10 disjoint time windows. Separately, the paper is paleoclimatology rather than biology, no approved pretrained backbone takes this data type, and an open CC-BY machine-learning workflow on 53 paired coral records already covers the task honestly. The data itself is exemplary - fully open, units and instrument precision declared per column - it simply contains no label.
